Life tables from death rates on any age axis

Source: R/derive-lifetable.R
life_table.Rd

Period life table for single or grouped ages with an open last interval. Interval widths come from the age axis, so abridged and single-year schedules are handled by the same code. The relations are the standard ones of Preston, Heuveline and Guillot (2001):

Usage

life_table(
  mx,
  age = NULL,
  ax = NULL,
  open = c("reciprocal", "gompertz", "kannisto", "makeham", "weibull", "beard",
    "logquad", "logistic", "perks", "lynch_brown", "aic"),
  k = 10,
  radix = 1e+05,
  omega = 110,
  exposure = NULL
)

Arguments

mx

Death rates, one per interval of age.

age

An mt_axis (default: single ages from 0 with an open last interval).

ax

Optional average years lived in the interval by those who die.

open

"reciprocal", a hazard law ("gompertz", "kannisto", "makeham", "weibull", "beard", "logquad", "logistic", "perks", "lynch_brown") or "aic".

k

Number of ages used for the fit of a hazard law.

radix

Starting number of survivors.

omega

Age up to which a fitted hazard is applied (default 110, the default omega of mt_data()); ignored with open = "reciprocal".

exposure

Optional person-years of the age intervals, which weight the maximum-likelihood fit of a hazard law with the observed numbers at risk; by default the numbers of the life table. Needed for open = "aic".

Value

A data.table with age_lo, age_hi, n, mx, ax, qx, lx, dx, Lx, Tx, ex. With a Gompertz or Kannisto closure, the attribute "tail" holds the fitted a and b, the ages of the fit and whether it converged. With another law it holds alpha, beta, gamma and delta (NA where the law has fewer parameters), the log-likelihood loglik and aic (with exposure only), the ages and converged; with "aic" one such row per law, with delta_aic and the selected law.

Details

  • q_x = n m / (1 + (n - a) m) for a closed interval of width n; where this exceeds 1 (rates above about 2 / n, far beyond observed values), the constant-hazard value 1 - exp(-n m) is used, so that survivors stay positive;

  • a_x defaults to n / 2 for every closed interval, the simple convention of deaths spread evenly over the interval (supply ax to override). At age 0, n / 2 overstates the average time lived by infants who die; the Human Mortality Database uses the age-0 values of Andreev and Kingkade (2015), which depend on sex and on the infant death rate and are not implemented here. The effect on e0 at low infant mortality is below 0.01 years;

  • open interval: "reciprocal" (default) uses L = l / m (Preston, Heuveline and Guillot 2001). "gompertz" and "kannisto" close the table with the Gompertz hazard mu(x) = a exp(b x) or the Kannisto hazard mu(x) = a exp(b x) / (1 + a exp(b x)), whose logit is linear in age and which levels off at old ages (Thatcher, Kannisto and Vaupel 1998, chapter 2). They are fitted as in Thatcher, Kannisto and Vaupel (1998, chapter 6), by maximum likelihood with binomial deaths: of the N persons who reach age x, d die before x + 1 with probability q = 1 - exp(-H), where H is the integral of the hazard over the year. The fit uses the last k closed single-year ages. N and d are the survivors and deaths of the life table itself, the numbers of a stationary population with these rates, unless exposure gives the observed person-years E (then d = m E and N = E + (1 - a) d). Thatcher et al. fit observed numbers, at ages 80 to 98; the life-table numbers are a package-specific choice for schedules without counts (reference unknown). For the cohorts born in 1871-1880 the life-table numbers are the observed ones, and the fit reproduces the published parameters (their Appendix D) from their probabilities of dying (Table 6.1). Earlier versions of mortensor fitted least squares to the log or logit rates. The fitted hazard is applied year by year from the start of the open interval to omega (survival exp(-H) and person-years l (1 - exp(-H)) / H in each year), and the survivors at omega are closed with L = l / H at the integrated hazard of the following year;

  • "makeham", "weibull", "beard", "logquad", "logistic", "perks" and "lynch_brown" close the table with the other hazard laws that Feehan (2018, Table 1 and Appendix E) compares, for age x in years:

    • Makeham: gamma + alpha exp(beta x);

    • Weibull: alpha x^(beta - 1) with x the age, as Thatcher et al. (1998) fit a x^b (Feehan's fits count age 80 as z = 1, Appendix E.9, which changes this law only);

    • Beard (gamma-Gompertz): alpha exp(beta x) / (1 + delta exp(beta x));

    • log-quadratic: exp(alpha + beta x + gamma x^2) (the quadratic model of Coale and Kisker in Thatcher et al. 1998);

    • logistic: gamma + alpha exp(beta x) / (1 + delta exp(beta x)) (the logistic model of Thatcher et al. 1998 in another parameterisation);

    • Perks (gamma-Makeham): (gamma + alpha exp(beta x)) / (1 + delta exp(beta x));

    • Lynch-Brown: alpha + beta atan(gamma (x - delta)).

    The parameters are positive, except beta of Makeham, all parameters of the log-quadratic law and alpha and delta of Lynch-Brown, which are real (Feehan's Appendix E). They are fitted by the same binomial maximum likelihood as the Kannisto closure, with the integrated hazards of Feehan's Appendix E in closed form (for the log-quadratic law by Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 20 nodes per year, as its closed form needs the error function of an imaginary argument when gamma > 0). Feehan maximises with BFGS from one heuristic and ten random starts; the package takes Levenberg-Marquardt steps on the Fisher information from several deterministic starts and keeps the highest likelihood (package-specific, reference unknown);

  • "aic" fits all nine laws and closes each schedule with the law of the lowest Akaike information criterion, AIC = -2 loglik + 2 k with k parameters, the criterion by which Feehan (2018, section 4.2) compares the models. It needs exposure: with the numbers of the life table (radix 1) the likelihood has no sample size;

  • a rate of 0 in the open interval (no deaths, as in small populations) would give an infinite life expectancy: the last positive rate of the closed intervals is used for the open interval instead (column mx keeps the given rate). Only a schedule without any positive rate gives an infinite value.

References

Andreev EM, Kingkade WW (2015). Average age at death in infancy and infant mortality level: reconsidering the Coale-Demeny formulas at current levels of low mortality. Demographic Research 33: 363-390.

Feehan DM (2018). Separating the signal from the noise: evidence for deceleration in old-age death rates. Demography 55(6): 2025-2044. doi:10.1007/s13524-018-0728-x

Preston SH, Heuveline P, Guillot M (2001). Demography: Measuring and Modeling Population Processes. Blackwell.

Thatcher AR, Kannisto V, Vaupel JW (1998). The Force of Mortality at Ages 80 to 120. Odense University Press.

See also

mt_open_check() to compare the laws out of sample.

Examples

m <- 3e-4 + 2e-5 * exp(0.1 * (30:100))
lt <- life_table(m, single_ages(30, 100))
lt[age_lo %in% c(30, 65, 100)]
#>    age_lo age_hi     n           mx       ax           qx         lx         dx
#>     <num>  <num> <num>        <num>    <num>        <num>      <num>      <num>
#> 1:     30     31     1 0.0007017107 0.500000 0.0007014646 100000.000   70.14646
#> 2:     65     66     1 0.0136028327 0.500000 0.0135109391  87531.735 1182.63594
#> 3:    100    Inf   Inf 0.4408293159 2.268452 1.0000000000   1460.141 1460.14118
#>          Lx         Tx        ex
#>       <num>      <num>     <num>
#> 1: 99964.93 4973452.39 49.734524
#> 2: 86940.42 1596839.74 18.242981
#> 3:  3312.26    3312.26  2.268452
# Kannisto closure fitted by maximum likelihood to ages 90-99
lk <- life_table(m, single_ages(30, 100), open = "kannisto")
attr(lk, "tail")
#>         law            a         b age_from age_to converged
#>      <char>        <num>     <num>    <num>  <num>    <lgcl>
#> 1: kannisto 1.045127e-06 0.1338894       90    100      TRUE
# the log-quadratic law of Feehan (2018)
attr(life_table(m, single_ages(30, 100), open = "logquad"), "tail")
#>        law     alpha       beta        gamma delta loglik   aic age_from age_to
#>     <char>     <num>      <num>        <num> <num>  <num> <num>    <num>  <num>
#> 1: logquad -9.903961 0.07871943 0.0001176787    NA     NA    NA       90    100
#>    converged
#>       <lgcl>
#> 1:      TRUE
